tests.title: Sharing housework: the problem and two projects

groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Why do household tasks on Rote take a long time?

evidence.summary: Limited washing equipment and the absence of running water make the work time-consuming.

distractors.B: The programme attributes the time needed to limited facilities, not a repeated-washing rule.
distractors.C: A shortage is described, not a ban on using machines.

options.label: A
options.text: There are few washing machines and no running water.

options.label: B
options.text: The project asks families to wash everything twice.

options.label: C
options.text: The island's workers are forbidden to use machines.

questions.prompt: What does the NGO project try to change?

evidence.summary: The project is explicitly concerned with attitudes towards women's roles.

distractors.A: Rice farming is background context, not the project's stated target.
distractors.B: The project is not described as setting children's leaving age.

options.label: A
options.text: The crops grown by the island's rice farmers.

options.label: B
options.text: The age at which children leave the family home.

options.label: C
options.text: Attitudes towards the role of the island's women.

questions.prompt: What extra work does Shilpa say women do?

evidence.summary: Women's field work challenges the idea that the household division is already fair.

distractors.A: No condition that men must be away is attached to this statement.
distractors.C: The report describes work in fields alongside domestic work, not only office work.

options.label: A
options.text: They only work when the men are away fishing.

options.label: B
options.text: They help in the fields as well as at home.

options.label: C
options.text: They only do paid office work.

questions.prompt: How does the second listener describe the arrangement with her husband?

evidence.summary: The second listener reports an unequal division in which she does most chores.

distractors.B: She explicitly denies that the chores are shared equally.
distractors.C: Her statement concerns chores, not a comparison of paid working hours.

options.label: B

questions.prompt: What does Neil use to explain his household's arrangement?

evidence.summary: Neil relates task-sharing to the different paid-work schedules of the two partners.

distractors.A: He distinguishes part-time from full-time work rather than identical hours.
distractors.B: He explains availability around work, not a preference-only allocation.

options.label: A
options.text: Both partners have identical paid working hours.

options.label: B
options.text: Their tasks are divided solely according to preference.

options.label: C
options.text: Each partner does tasks when not occupied by paid work.

questions.prompt: What does the UN Women figure compare?

evidence.summary: The three-hour figure is a daily difference between women's and men's unpaid work.

distractors.A: The statistic concerns time on unpaid care and domestic work, not equipment ownership.
distractors.C: The time unit is each day, not an entire working lifetime.

options.label: A
options.text: The number of women and men who own washing machines.

options.label: B
options.text: Women's daily unpaid work time with men's.

options.label: C
options.text: Women's total working lifetime with men's.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Why is the apparent fairness of the island's division questioned?

evidence.summary: The account challenges a simple home-versus-fields division because women contribute to both.

distractors.A: The lack of equipment and water makes domestic work especially time-consuming.
distractors.C: The report says men work in the fields and women help there too.

options.label: A
options.text: Domestic work is said to require no time.

options.label: B
options.text: Women also contribute to the work outside the home.

options.label: C
options.text: Men do no work in the fields.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the reference to wealthy countries?

evidence.summary: The comparison extends the issue beyond the traditional-society setting.

distractors.B: The programme reports inequality in wealthy countries rather than making that guarantee.
distractors.C: It specifically says women there still spend more time on unpaid care.

options.label: A
options.text: To show that the imbalance is not confined to traditional societies.

options.label: B
options.text: To show that running water guarantees equal housework.

options.label: C
options.text: To show that unpaid care work disappears as countries become wealthier.

tests.title: Fair sharing: separating assumptions from evidence

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.prompt: Final example in the first listener's list: cleaning the {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Her list ends with bathroom cleaning after shopping and cooking.

questions.prompt: Paid-work pattern Neil attributes to his wife: {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Neil identifies his wife's work as part time, distinguishing it from his own schedule.

questions.prompt: Reported daily difference in unpaid work: {{blank}} hours.

evidence.summary: The figure is an excess of three hours relative to men, not the total amount of women's unpaid work.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: Which connection does the report make between resources and workload?

evidence.summary: The practical resource limitations are presented as a reason chores take a long time.

distractors.A: No link between fishing and workshop numbers is made.
distractors.C: Household care remains part of the workload despite agricultural work.

options.label: A
options.text: The presence of fishermen determines how many workshops take place.

options.label: B
options.text: Scarce washing equipment and absent piped water lengthen domestic tasks.

options.label: C
options.text: Working in rice fields removes the need for household care.

questions.prompt: Which description stays closest to the first project's stated approach?

evidence.summary: The approach combines local community partners with an attempt to change role expectations.

distractors.B: The NGO works alongside the leaders rather than replacing them.
distractors.C: The stated aim is attitude change, not a new fishing-employment scheme.

options.label: A
options.text: Working with local leaders to change perceptions of women's roles.

options.label: B
options.text: Replacing local leaders with visiting household workers.

options.label: C
options.text: Providing new fishing jobs as the main way to reduce women's workload.

questions.prompt: Which fact undermines the suggestion that the division is already equitable?

evidence.summary: Women's participation in both domains weakens the simple claim of an already fair division.

distractors.A: Men's outside work is the basis of the initial suggestion, not the fact that qualifies it.
distractors.B: The care responsibilities describe the domestic load but do not alone reveal women's additional field work.

options.label: A
options.text: Men traditionally work in rice farming or fishing.

options.label: B
options.text: Children and older people are among those requiring care.

options.label: C
options.text: Women contribute in the fields as well as being expected to handle the home.

groups.heading: Questions 9–10
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: How should the comment about women nagging less be reported?

evidence.summary: The explicit joking qualification limits how the remark should be interpreted and attributed.

distractors.A: The speaker reports a joke and uses a tendency, not universal proof.
distractors.B: No numerical evaluation measure or universal workshop criterion is provided.

options.label: A
options.text: As proof that every participating family has eliminated disagreements.

options.label: B
options.text: As the measured outcome by which all workshops are judged.

options.label: C
options.text: As a joking remark in the account, not a quantified result about all women.

questions.prompt: What common conclusion links the two projects despite their different settings?

evidence.summary: The common conclusion links more domestic help from men with happier households.

distractors.B: The projects aim to change imbalances rather than reproduce a single traditional arrangement.
distractors.C: Resource limits feature in one setting, but identical equipment is not their shared conclusion.

options.label: A
options.text: Greater male participation in domestic tasks is associated with happier homes.

options.label: B
options.text: Household happiness depends on reproducing the same traditional roles everywhere.

options.label: C
options.text: Equal sharing requires every household to use the same appliances.
